subs.text: Book twenty-three.
The Great Rooted Bed.
Scene one.
Eurycleia Wakes Penelope.
Wake, my child, wake and see it with your own eyes.
Odysseus is home, here in this house, and every suitor lies dead in the hall.
The man you have mourned twenty years is sitting by his own fire.
Penelope first thinks the nurse has gone mad or that a god punished the men.
Eurycleia offers the scar as proof and describes the king waiting below.
Penelope descends, divided between embracing him and testing him from a distance.

She and Odysseus share private signs.

subs.text: Scene four.
The Bed Test.
Move the marriage bed outside the chamber for the stranger.
Woman, who has moved my bed?
I built it myself around a living olive trunk still rooted in the ground, and I roofed the chamber over it.
No man alive could shift that bed without taking an axe to the tree.
The secret proves identity.
Penelope runs to him and embraces him.
Fear of deception caused her delay.
Athena holds back dawn while husband and wife weep and reunite.

scenes.title: Odysseus Tells the Remaining Journey
scenes.card: In bed, husband and wife tell each other their years apart; he admits one last journey still awaits him.

subs.text: Scene five.
Odysseus Tells the Remaining Journey.
In bed Odysseus and Penelope recount the years they spent apart.
Travel inland with an oar and appease Poseidon.
Odysseus describes the eventual gentle death foretold for him.
If the gods have set a better old age at the end of that road, then go when you must go.
I have waited before;
I know the shape of waiting.
Only come back to this bed.
Penelope sleep while Athena finally releases the dawn.

At dawn Odysseus arms himself with Telemachus, Eumaeus, and Philoetius.
Stay within doors, all of you, and bar them;
let no woman lean out to look.
Word of the dead will run through the town before noon.
See nothing, say nothing, until I send for you.
